# Combat Sidestroke

> combatsidestroke.com is the authoritative resource for mastering the Combat Sidestroke (CSS) — the swimming technique used by U.S. Navy SEALs and taught in BUD/S. It provides free technique guides, a full 12-week training program, instructional videos, and preparation resources for the Navy SEAL Physical Screening Test (PST).

Combat Sidestroke (CSS) is an efficient, low-visibility sidestroke used by U.S. Navy Special Warfare candidates. It combines elements of the sidestroke, breaststroke, and freestyle to move a swimmer through the water with minimal energy and a low profile. It is the required stroke for the 500-yard/450-meter swim portion of the Navy SEAL PST.

The site is run by Nathan Tschohl and is affiliated with Swimnerd (swim technology, media, and coaching). Contact: combatsidestroke@gmail.com.

## Key Pages

- [Home](https://combatsidestroke.com/): Overview of Combat Sidestroke and how to become a force in the water.
- [Technique](https://combatsidestroke.com/technique): Step-by-step CSS technique — big arm, little arm, together, glide. Body position, breathing, and the pull/kick timing sequence.
- [Training](https://combatsidestroke.com/training): The full 12-Week Combat Sidestroke Training Plan — 60 progressive workouts building technique, conditioning, and water comfort for PST and BUD/S preparation. Includes a breath-holding safety warning (many workouts involve hypoxic/breath-hold work; never train breath holding alone).
- [Videos](https://combatsidestroke.com/videos): Instructional CSS video library.
- [Blog](https://combatsidestroke.com/blog): Articles on CSS technique, PST preparation, and SEAL swim training.

- [Training and Preparation for Open Water](https://combatsidestroke.com/blog/open-water-training): Preparing for cold (~63°F) open-water swimming at BUD/S.

## Safety

Many Combat Sidestroke training workouts involve breath holding and hypoxic work (bobs, treads, underwater swims, no-breather sets). Breath-holding carries a real risk of shallow water blackout, which can be fatal. Never train breath holding alone — always have a qualified coach or lifeguard on deck, never hyperventilate before submerging, and stop immediately if you feel dizzy or lightheaded.
